title: Non-Alcoholic Fatty Liver Disease
subject: Medicine
summary: Non-Alcoholic Fatty Liver Disease (NAFLD) is the most common metabolic liver disease, characterized by fat accumulation in the liver in individuals who consume minimal or no alcohol. It is strongly linked to obesity, type 2 diabetes, and insulin resistance. NAFLD can progress to inflammation (NASH), fibrosis, cirrhosis, and end-stage liver disease.

sections.p: Non-Alcoholic Fatty Liver Disease (NAFLD) is defined by the presence of hepatic steatosis (fat in the liver) in individuals who do not consume significant amounts of alcohol. Significant alcohol consumption is typically defined as more than 20g/day for women and more than 30g/day for men. Diagnosis requires imaging evidence of steatosis and exclusion of other causes of liver disease, particularly viral hepatitis and significant alcohol use.
b: Hepatic steatosis on imaging (e.g., ultrasound).
Minimal or no significant alcohol consumption.
Exclusion of other causes of liver disease (e.g., viral hepatitis B/C, autoimmune liver disease, drug-induced liver injury).

sections.p: NAFLD encompasses a spectrum from simple steatosis (NAFL) to non-alcoholic steatohepatitis (NASH), which involves inflammation and hepatocyte injury, with or without fibrosis. NASH can progress to cirrhosis and hepatocellular carcinoma. Staging involves assessing the degree of fibrosis, which is the most important predictor of long-term outcomes.
b: NAFL (Non-Alcoholic Fatty Liver): Simple steatosis without inflammation or hepatocyte injury.
NASH (Non-Alcoholic Steatohepatitis): Steatosis with inflammation and hepatocyte injury, potentially leading to fibrosis.
Fibrosis: Scarring of the liver, staged from F0 (no fibrosis) to F4 (cirrhosis).

sections.p: NAFLD is primarily a manifestation of metabolic syndrome. The most common underlying causes are related to lifestyle and metabolic dysregulation.
b: Obesity: Strongest risk factor, especially central obesity.
Type 2 Diabetes Mellitus: High prevalence of NAFLD in diabetic patients, often linked to insulin resistance.
Insulin Resistance: A key pathophysiological driver, leading to increased free fatty acid delivery to the liver.
Dyslipidaemia: High triglycerides and low HDL cholesterol.
Metabolic Syndrome: Co-occurrence of obesity, diabetes, hypertension, and dyslipidaemia.
Certain medications: Glucocorticoids, amiodarone, tamoxifen (less common than metabolic causes).
HIV: HIV infection and some antiretroviral therapies can contribute to metabolic dysfunction and NAFLD.

sections.p: Most patients with NAFLD are asymptomatic, especially in the early stages. Symptoms, when present, are often non-specific and may indicate more advanced disease or complications.
b: Often asymptomatic, discovered incidentally on imaging or abnormal liver function tests.
Fatigue and malaise: Non-specific symptoms, common in many chronic conditions.
Right upper quadrant discomfort: Mild, dull ache, usually not severe.
Hepatomegaly: Palpable liver edge, often smooth and non-tender, indicating fatty infiltration.
Signs of advanced liver disease (cirrhosis): Jaundice, ascites, peripheral oedema, spider naevi, palmar erythema (in later stages).

sections.p: Investigations aim to diagnose steatosis, assess for inflammation and fibrosis, and exclude other causes of liver disease. In low-resource settings, initial investigations focus on readily available tests.

t.a: Liver Function Tests (LFTs): ALT, AST, ALP, GGT, Bilirubin, Albumin

sections.p: While often benign, NAFLD can progress to serious complications, particularly when it advances to NASH and cirrhosis. Clinicians must be vigilant for signs of decompensation.
b: Progressive fatigue, weakness, or unexplained weight loss.
Jaundice (yellowing of skin/eyes): Sign of severe liver dysfunction.
Ascites (abdominal swelling due to fluid accumulation): Indicates portal hypertension and decompensated cirrhosis.
Peripheral oedema: Swelling in legs/ankles, often with ascites.
Hepatic encephalopathy: Confusion, disorientation, altered mental status due to liver failure.
Gastrointestinal bleeding (e.g., haematemesis, melaena): Suggests variceal bleeding from portal hypertension.
Hepatocellular carcinoma (HCC): Risk increases significantly with cirrhosis.

sections.p: Management of NAFLD focuses on treating the underlying metabolic risk factors and preventing progression to advanced liver disease. There are no specific drugs approved solely for NAFLD, so lifestyle modification is paramount.
b: Lifestyle modification: Cornerstone of treatment. Includes gradual weight loss (7-10% of body weight), regular physical activity, and a healthy diet (e.g., reduced refined carbohydrates and saturated fats).
Manage co-morbidities: Strict control of blood glucose in diabetes, blood pressure in hypertension, and lipid levels in dyslipidaemia. Metformin can be beneficial for insulin resistance and diabetes.
Avoid hepatotoxic agents: Minimize alcohol intake (even small amounts can be detrimental), avoid unnecessary medications, and herbal remedies without proven safety.
Vaccinations: Hepatitis A and B vaccinations are crucial to prevent additional liver insults.
Vitamin E: May be considered in non-diabetic adults with biopsy-proven NASH, but evidence is mixed and not universally recommended due to potential risks.
Pioglitazone: May be considered in patients with biopsy-proven NASH, especially those with type 2 diabetes, but has side effects (weight gain, fluid retention, bone fractures).

sections.p: Regular follow-up is essential to monitor disease progression, manage co-morbidities, and screen for complications. Prevention focuses on addressing metabolic risk factors in the general population.
b: Regular monitoring of LFTs, blood glucose, and lipid profile.
Periodic imaging (e.g., ultrasound) to assess for changes in steatosis or signs of cirrhosis.
Screening for hepatocellular carcinoma in patients with cirrhosis (e.g., ultrasound every 6 months).
Patient education on diet, exercise, and weight management.
Early identification and management of metabolic syndrome in primary care settings.

sections.p: NAFLD can be confused with other causes of fatty liver or chronic liver disease, especially given the non-specific nature of its early presentation.
b: Alcoholic Fatty Liver Disease (AFLD): Histologically similar, but distinguished by significant alcohol consumption. History is key.
Viral Hepatitis (B and C): Can also cause chronic liver inflammation and fibrosis. Excluded by serological tests.
Drug-induced Liver Injury (DILI): Certain medications can cause steatosis or hepatitis. A thorough medication history is important.
Autoimmune Hepatitis: Can present with elevated LFTs. Distinguished by autoantibodies and often more severe inflammation.
Haemochromatosis: Iron overload can cause liver damage. Distinguished by elevated ferritin and transferrin saturation.
Wilson's Disease: Copper overload. Rare, but can cause liver disease in younger individuals.

sections.p: Several aspects of NAFLD diagnosis and assessment can be misleading, requiring careful clinical interpretation.
b: Normal liver function tests: Up to 80% of patients with NAFLD, and even some with NASH or advanced fibrosis, can have normal ALT/AST levels. Normal LFTs do not rule out significant liver disease.
Ultrasound sensitivity: Ultrasound can miss mild steatosis (less than 20-30% fat infiltration) and is not reliable for assessing inflammation or fibrosis.
Biopsy variability: Liver biopsy is invasive and subject to sampling error, as steatosis and fibrosis can be patchy.

Non-invasive fibrosis scores: While helpful, these scores are screening tools and can have false positives or negatives, especially in intermediate risk categories. They are not definitive for ruling out advanced fibrosis.

whenToSeekHelp: Yellowing of the skin or eyes (jaundice)
Swelling in the legs or ankles (oedema)
Confusion, disorientation, or changes in personality (hepatic encephalopathy)
Vomiting blood or passing black, tarry stools (gastrointestinal bleeding)
Severe, persistent fatigue or unexplained weight loss

faq.a: Yes, simple steatosis (NAFL) can often be reversed with significant lifestyle changes, particularly weight loss and dietary modifications. NASH with mild fibrosis may also improve, but advanced fibrosis and cirrhosis are generally irreversible.

No, many people with NAFLD have simple fatty liver (NAFL) which is often benign and does not progress. However, a significant proportion can develop NASH, which carries a risk of progression to cirrhosis and liver failure.

faq.q: What is the role of alcohol in NAFLD?
faq.a: By definition, NAFLD occurs in individuals with minimal or no significant alcohol consumption. If there is significant alcohol intake, the condition is termed Alcoholic Fatty Liver Disease (AFLD). However, even moderate alcohol consumption in someone with NAFLD can worsen liver damage.

exam: A 45-year-old obese woman with type 2 diabetes presents with mild right upper quadrant discomfort and fatigue. Her LFTs show ALT 60 U/L (normal <40), AST 50 U/L (normal <40). What is your initial diagnostic approach, especially considering a low-resource setting? — Focus on history for alcohol, medications, and risk factors. You diagnose NAFLD in a patient. What are the key lifestyle modifications you would advise, and why are they crucial? — Emphasize gradual weight loss (7-10% of body weight) through diet and exercise. Explain that weight loss improves insulin sensitivity, reduces hepatic fat accumulation, and can reverse steatosis and improve inflammation.

A patient with known NAFLD develops jaundice, ascites, and confusion. What do these signs indicate, and what is your immediate management priority? — These are signs of decompensated cirrhosis. Immediate priorities include stabilizing the patient, assessing for precipitating factors (e.g., infection, GI bleed), and managing complications like ascites (diuretics), encephalopathy (lactulose), and potential variceal bleeding.

How would you differentiate NAFLD from Alcoholic Fatty Liver Disease (AFLD) in a patient presenting with fatty liver on ultrasound? — The primary differentiator is a detailed alcohol history. Quantify daily/weekly alcohol intake. Acknowledge that patients may underreport, so collateral history or screening tools might be helpful. Explain that histology can be identical, making history paramount.

A patient's LFTs are consistently normal, but an abdominal ultrasound shows significant hepatic steatosis. Can you still diagnose NAFLD, and what is the clinical significance of normal LFTs in this context? — Yes, NAFLD can be diagnosed. Normal LFTs do not rule out NAFLD or even advanced fibrosis/NASH. Explain that LFTs reflect hepatocyte injury, not necessarily fat content or fibrosis, and many patients with NAFLD have normal enzymes.

What are the non-invasive methods available to assess fibrosis in NAFLD, and how would you use them in a setting where liver biopsy is not readily available? — Discuss non-invasive scores like FIB-4 or NAFLD Fibrosis Score (calculated from routine labs). Explain their role in risk stratification to identify patients at higher risk of advanced fibrosis who may need closer follow-up or referral if possible.
